title: Pattern repeat notation
subtitle: How asterisk, bracket, and parenthesis notations tell you where to repeat a stitch sequence
excerpt: Crochet patterns use three different symbols to mark a repeating stitch sequence. All three mean the same thing. Learn to read each format and you can follow any pattern's repeat instructions.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A sequence of stitches that is worked a set number of times. Enclosed in asterisks, brackets, or parentheses in written patterns.
The minimum number of stitches required for a stitch repeat to work out evenly, sometimes with a stated remainder added to the foundation chain.

aliases: how to follow a crochet repeat

content.text: A
stitch repeat

is a sequence of stitches that you work more than once across a row or round. Patterns mark the sequence boundaries using one of three notations: asterisks (*), square brackets ([]), or round brackets/parentheses. All three mean the same thing: work the stitches between the markers, then repeat them the stated number of times or until the row end.
Asterisk notation
Asterisks mark the start and sometimes the end of the repeat.
* 1 tr, ch 1; rep from * to last st: work 1 treble and chain 1, then repeat that pair from the asterisk to the last stitch.
* 2 dc, sk 1 *; rep from * to * 5 times: work the sequence between the two asterisks, five times in total.
Bracket notation
Brackets show the repeat inline.
[2 tr in next st, sk 1] 4 times: work the content of the square brackets four times.
[dc, ch 2] across: repeat the bracketed sequence to the end of the row.
Round bracket notation
Round brackets can mean either a stitch repeat or a stitch count at the row end. Check the context.
(1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) 3 times: a stitch repeat, worked three times.
(30 sts): a stitch count at the end of the row, confirming how many stitches the row should contain.
The repeat multiple
A stitch repeat that uses 4 stitches requires a foundation chain that is a
multiple of 4

. Some patterns add a stated remainder: 'multiple of 4 + 2'. This means the chain needs to be a multiple of 4 plus 2 extra stitches (6, 10, 14, 18, and so on). The pattern's 'materials' or 'notes' section usually states the multiple if one is required.
Common problems

items.symptom: The repeat runs out before the end of the row
items.cause: The foundation chain is not a multiple of the repeat.
items.fix: Count the stitches in the repeat and check the foundation chain is divisible by that number (plus any stated remainder). Adjust the chain before starting the first row.

items.symptom: The row ends with half a repeat left over
items.cause: The wrong number of times was repeated for the row width.
items.fix: Count from the start of the row, tracking each full repeat until the markers run out. If partial repeat remains, the foundation chain stitch count may be wrong.

content.text: What to try next

Find a simple lace pattern that uses both asterisk and bracket notation in the same row instructions. Reading the two formats in the same row, side by side, makes clear that they do the same job. A granny square pattern is a good starting point as it uses all three formats within a short set of instructions.
